source.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Michael Lan; P. Torr; Austin Meek; Ashkan Khakzar; David Krueger; Fazl Barez

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests a qualified form of feature universality and argues that it is weak and incomplete: selected SAE feature subspaces align, but the paper does not claim convergence to identical features or alignment across entire feature spaces.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own cross-model and cross-seed SAE similarity results, so rows are included for those. Background and results cited from other work are excluded. Many layer-pair heatmap cells and appendix comparisons are omitted; values used only for selecting feature pairs or filters are not treated as similarity outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study uses its own method to measure whether SAE feature subspaces are similar across different LLMs, which bears on V5. It pairs SAE features by activation correlation, then compares the paired decoder-weight spaces with SVCCA and RSA against a random-pairing null. The two measures give very different magnitudes, and scores depend on layer, filtering and SAE quality, which bears on V6. The authors also state that large parts of the feature spaces do not match, which bears on V7. The paper frames its result as positive evidence for weak universality, so T2 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that SVCCA shows high similarity between activation-correlated SAE feature subspaces across LLMs, especially in middle layers. Semantic subspaces such as calendar and people are particularly similar, which they take as evidence of weak, analogous feature-space universality. They add that RSA similarity is much weaker and parts of the feature spaces do not match. A notable fraction of features is idiosyncratic, and SAEs capture shared features inconsistently. They explicitly do not claim, as Huh et al. do, that models converge.
record.recipe_differences: Features are paired by activation correlation, then compared using SVCCA and RSA on SAE decoder-weight representations. The paper contrasts this with approaches comparing activations for already paired input samples.
record.method_sensitivity: Scores vary by similarity measure (SVCCA versus RSA), layer pair, semantic category, feature-pair filtering and mapping type. The paper also reports that the quality and training data of the SAE affect which similarities are revealed, and that changing the dataset used to obtain activations produces broadly similar results with some scores slightly higher on OpenWebText.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained with different seeds on the same fixed model give partly similar feature-space scores. Same-layer SVCCA across seeds averages 0.376 on Pythia-70m but reaches 0.94 on TinyStories after filtering. SAE quality strongly changes the similarity revealed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different SAE training runs on one fixed model expose partly similar feature subspaces; how similar depends on SAE quality and training data.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on a randomized Pythia-70m show very low similarity to SAEs trained on the trained model, and only about 1% of pairs are kept. This is used as a control.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model SAE feature-space similarity reflects learned computation, not only sparse token statistics.

record.problems: The study analyzes only a sample of SAEs and models with the same tokenizer, uses limited activation datasets, and relies on feature pairing and filtering choices. It states that similarity measures depend on pairing quality, SAEs may capture different features inconsistently, and generalization to more diverse datasets or domain-specific models is open. It does not measure model capability or a scale-performance trend.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted many separate layer-pair values shown in Figures 2-5 and appendix heatmaps, the additional semantic-category heatmaps and p-value plots, and most appendix comparisons varying SAE width, SAE training data, activation dataset, token count, or mapping direction. These would substantially exceed a concise catalog; the text-explicit values, principal semantic tables, metric comparison, and relevant partial/challenge results are retained.

untested.parts: Compares some differently sized models (70m vs 160m, 2B vs 9B) but reports no trend of alignment with scale or capability.
No vision-language or paired image-caption comparison.
Only SAE seeds are varied on a fixed network; no networks trained from different initializations.
No map, stitching, transfer loss or unpaired alignment is evaluated. Transferability is only suggested as an implication.
Only same-tokenizer, mostly same-family transformer LLMs are compared. Identical features or circuits are not tested; the paper explicitly measures weak or analogous universality.
Neighbourhood-size settings and out-of-distribution inputs are not tested.
Plateau with scale and the shared-data or shared-objective explanation are not tested.

missing.what: Layer 0 is always non-significant, early layers score low, and middle layers score highest across all model pairs.
Only about 10-30% (typically 20%) of feature pairs are retained after non-concept and many-to-1 filtering.
1-1 vs many-to-1 pairing changes scores, e.g. Pythia L2 vs L3 SVCCA rises from 0.03 to 0.35. For semantic subspaces, 1-1 scores are vastly better.
Mean activation correlation does not track SVCCA: a pairing with correlation 0.6 can give SVCCA 0.03.
Changing the activation dataset (RedPajama vs OpenWebText) or the token count gives broadly similar results.
Cross-model comparisons using lower-quality custom SAEs keep only 2-4% of pairs and give very low RSA, with moderate SVCCA only in some layers.
Base vs instruct models: Gemma-1-2B vs its instruct version reaches SVCCA 0.84 (random 0.008) and RSA 0.25. Gemma-2-9B vs 9B-IT is shown in Figure 5.
Test 2 (semantic subspaces vs random subsets of the same size) passes for all layers and concept categories.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the tranche from T5 to T2 because the paper's main framing is positive evidence obtained with a new method. I replaced the reader's V6 'supports' label, which rested on above-random similarity: that is V5 evidence, not evidence of metric dependence. V6 support now rests on the SVCCA vs RSA gap. I unlinked r28 from V7 because it is a randomization control, not a test of the shared-data explanation. The V6 'limits_scope' label on activation-dataset robustness rests on text (Appendix G) that no row records; its row_ids are empty and it is listed under missing. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares some differently sized models, but does not test whether alignment rises as model scale and capability increase.
The different-seed experiments train SAEs on a fixed model; they do not train networks from different initializations.
The study measures rotation-invariant similarity after feature pairing, but does not evaluate a representation map, stitching, transfer loss, or alignment without paired data.
The study compares SAE feature subspaces and semantically selected groups; it does not establish that identical interpretable features or circuits recur.
The study compares SVCCA and RSA and varies some data and pairing choices, but does not systematically test neighbourhood-count settings or out-of-distribution inputs.
It reports incomplete and method-dependent similarity, but does not establish that shared training data or objectives cause alignment, or test a plateau in alignment as scale increases.

relationships.condition: SVCCA on 1-1 paired, filtered SAE features in middle layers: Pythia-70m vs 160m, Gemma-1-2B vs Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-2B vs 9B, across most semantic subspaces
relationships.reason: Paired SVCCA scores of 0.30-0.83 sit far above random-pairing means (0.05-0.15) with p≤0.01 (r1-r9, r11, r12, r20). RSA for MonthNames is 0.76 (r16).
relationships.display_finding: Paired SVCCA scores reached 0.30–0.83 versus random means of 0.05–0.15 with p≤0.01, while MonthNames RSA reached 0.76.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: SVCCA on 1-1 paired, filtered SAE features in middle layers: Pythia-70m vs 160m, Gemma-1-2B vs Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-2B vs 9B, across most semantic subspaces
source_check.reason: The selected semantic subspaces show analogous features above shuffled-pairing controls. The label is justified, but its significance summary must exclude r20: that comparison reports 10 random runs and no p-value, with random mean 0.009.

relationships.condition: RSA measure, the Gemma Countries subspace, the Llama later-layer pair, and early/layer-0 comparisons
relationships.reason: RSA similarity is much weaker than SVCCA: 0.09-0.46 vs 0.50-0.83 for the same subspaces, and 0.195 vs 0.70 for Gemma-2 (r13-r15, r17-r19, r21). Gemma Countries fails Test 1 (p=0.07, r10). Llama L25 reaches only 0.3 (r22). The text says layer 0 is never significant.
relationships.display_finding: RSA scored 0.09–0.46 versus SVCCA 0.50–0.83, including 0.195 versus 0.70 for Gemma-2; Gemma Countries failed significance at p=0.07, Llama layer 25 reached only 0.3, and layer 0 was never significant.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: RSA measure, the Gemma Countries subspace, the Llama later-layer pair, and early/layer-0 comparisons
source_check.reason: These conditions collectively qualify universality: RSA similarities are generally weaker, Gemma Countries fails Test 1, layer-0 comparisons are nonsignificant, and the Llama comparison yields 0.3 on only 7% retained pairs without a reported random baseline.

relationships.condition: SVCCA vs RSA on identical feature pairings
relationships.reason: For the same pairs, RSA gives far lower similarity than SVCCA (e.g. Time 0.10 vs 0.59; Gemma-2 0.195 vs 0.70), so the conclusion's strength depends on the measure (r1-r6, r13-r15, r17-r21). The text also reports dependence on layer, filtering, 1-1 vs many-to-1 pairing and SAE quality.
relationships.display_finding: RSA scored Time features at 0.10 versus SVCCA's 0.59 and Gemma-2 features at 0.195 versus 0.70; similarity also varied with layer, filtering, pairing strategy and SAE quality.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: SVCCA vs RSA on identical feature pairings
source_check.reason: Tables 1 and 9 give Time scores of 0.59 versus 0.10; Section 4.2 gives Gemma-2 scores of 0.70 versus 0.195. Sections 3 and 4.2 and Appendices J and K also establish sensitivity to pairing, filtering and layer.

relationships.condition: Choice of dataset and token count used to obtain activations for pairing
relationships.reason: Per Appendix G (no row records this), switching RedPajama to OpenWebText or raising tokens to 90k gives broadly similar scores. So data dependence does not extend to the activation dataset.
relationships.display_finding: Switching from RedPajama to OpenWebText or increasing the activation sample to 90,000 tokens produced broadly similar alignment scores.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Choice of dataset and token count used to obtain activations for pairing
source_check.reason: Appendix G reports broadly similar results across RedPajamas and OpenWebText and with 90k tokens, qualifying input dependence within these tested conditions. OpenWebText scores are slightly higher in most cases, and the 90k-token experiment has a layer-3 outlier.

relationships.reason: The authors state that many feature-space subsets do not match and that a notable fraction of features are idiosyncratic (r23). Per Section 4.2, only about 10-30% of pairs survive filtering.
relationships.display_finding: Many feature-space subsets failed to match, a notable fraction of features were idiosyncratic, and only about 10–30% of pairs survived filtering.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Section 4.2, the conclusion and Appendix H explicitly describe dissimilar feature-space subsets and idiosyncratic SAE features. This supports incomplete convergence; it does not establish shared-data or shared-objective causes, and SAE limitations remain an alternative explanation.

tranche.reason: The study tests feature universality using activation-based feature correspondence followed by representational comparison of SAE decoder weights, a different method addressing the convergence question.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is v4 dated 21 May 2025. Statement checks cover only this study's contributions; later-study Gemma figures are outside this audit. Universality here concerns analogous selected subspaces, not exact feature identity or demonstrated transfer.
